- (part 1 of 4) her rosary beads were always in her hands and her lips moving in prayers for her mother and for Brent Tarleton.

It did not occur to Debbie that Danielle had taken Brent’s death so seriously and that her grief was unhealed.

To Debbie, Danielle was still “baby sister,” far too young to have had a really serious love affair.

Debbie, standing in the sun in the cotton rows, her back breaking from the eternal bending and her hands roughened by the dry bolls, wished she had a sister who combined Hugo’s energy and strength with Danielle’s sweet disposition.

For Danielle picked diligently and earnestly.

But, after she had labored for an hour it was obvious that she, and not Hugo, was the one not yet well enough for such work.

So Debbie sent Danielle back to the house too.

There remained with her now in the long rows only Dilcey and Israel.

Israel picked lazily, spasmodically, complaining of her feet, her back, her internal miseries, her complete weariness, until her mother took a cotton stalk to her and whipped her until she screamed.

After that she worked a little better, taking care to stay far from her mother’s reach.
